source.version_note: Supplied arXiv:2102.09692v1 is a publisher-formatted accepted article with the PACM HCI citation and DOI printed on page 1. No later revision or separate second publication is counted.

citation.title: To Trust or to Think: Cognitive Forcing Functions Can Reduce Overreliance on AI in AI-assisted Decision-making
citation.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction 5(CSCW1), article 188

reading.source_scope_note: Human nutrition-task experiment with simulated AI advice, not a test of a learned model’s cognitive traits or clinical efficacy. Original Cacioppo–Petty trait-development papers and other cited primary studies were not independently read here.
access_limits: All 21 extracted pages read, including procedure, all six result tables, plots’ captions, individual-difference analysis, limitations and references. Table 2 on PDF page 11 was rendered and visually inspected; plots were not independently digitized.
Raw data, questionnaires beyond their reported items and analysis code were not obtained or rerun. The three additional exploratory interfaces were explicitly outside this paper’s reported results.

study.exclusions: 49 repeatedly chose ingredients absent from the image and had zero task accuracy; 12 assigned only to unreported exploratory conditions
study.design: Mixed incomplete between/within-subject assignment to two of nine interfaces; six analyzed conditions include no AI, two simple-explanation designs and three forcing designs
study.task: Replace the highest-carbohydrate ingredient and select a replacement optimizing a defined carbohydrate/flavor score
study.advice: Simulated 75%-accurate recognition, with controlled omissions generating incorrect advice
study.trait: Four-item need-for-cognition subset measured after the first block, then median-split

summary: Cognitive-forcing designs improved choices on incorrect-advice trials relative to simple explanations, but remained worse than no AI on those trials and did not significantly improve aggregate performance over simple explanations. Wrong-advice reliance declined significantly for identifying the carbohydrate source, not for every overall-decision reliance metric. Preference/trust and performance relationships were outcome-dependent. Need-for-cognition disaggregation suggested unequal benefits, without randomization of the trait.

findings.definition: A tendency to engage in and enjoy effortful thinking and cognitively demanding activities.
findings.novelty_rationale: Cognitive miserliness describes a shortcut-taking pattern; effort discounting concerns the cost of mental work. Need for cognition is a measured individual-difference construct concerning engagement and enjoyment, not the same failure mode or simply intelligence.

evidence.quote: how much a person enjoys engaging in cognitively demanding activities
at the median of the NFC

findings.evidence_scope: The study defines NFC from prior psychology and measures a four-item subset before disaggregating interface outcomes. It does not independently establish trait stability or a causal trait effect; the original trait-development papers were not read in this step.
findings.boundary: NFC differs from intelligence, expertise, current workload, compulsory reasoning effort and the accuracy of a particular answer. Low scores do not imply incapacity, poor moral character or a basis for withholding assistance. Model verbosity and self-reported enjoyment are not evidence that an AI possesses this human trait.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human trait measured in a controlled simulated-AI task; persistent functional AI analogue and subjective enjoyment untested
findings.ai_proposal: Untested functional AI analogue: across tasks with matched competence and explicit resource budgets, measure whether an assistant voluntarily chooses an informative but effortful verification step when a cheaper unsupported answer is available. Control prompt incentives, difficulty, latency and token limits; describe observable checking choices rather than attribute enjoyment or a stable personality.

findings.term: Cognitive forcing reduces some wrong-advice reliance without eliminating it
findings.definition: Decision-time interventions can improve rejection of incorrect simulated advice on selected measures while leaving residual overreliance and no significant overall advantage over simpler assistance.
findings.novelty_rationale: A tested intervention boundary within automation bias, not a new behaviour named after each interface.

evidence.quote: They also overrelied less, but not significantly so.
Our results did not provide support for the hypothesis (H1b)

findings.evidence_scope: The cognitive-forcing category combines on-demand, initial-independent-decision/update, and a 30-second wait. It improves wrong-advice-trial choices and carbohydrate-source reliance, but not aggregate performance versus the simple-explanation category; individual designs were not significantly differentiated.
findings.boundary: Do not replace every accuracy, reliance or subjective outcome with one positive headline. Group no-AI comparisons do not reveal each aided individual’s personal counterfactual. User trust, preference and usability are not validated substitutes for error correction.

findings.term: Effortful engagement and stated interface preference can diverge
findings.definition: Users may prefer or trust an easier interface while performing worse with it when the advice is incorrect; greater perceived effort can accompany better checking in that subset.
findings.novelty_rationale: Adds a bounded human interaction finding to effort-related decision behaviour, not a universal law that harder interfaces or longer deliberation are better.

evidence.quote: Trust and preference were significantly negatively correlated

findings.evidence_scope: Post-task subjective ratings correlated with selected wrong-advice performance measures. Aggregate CFF-versus-SXAI trust/preference comparisons were not all significant, and cognitive engagement was inferred rather than directly traced.
findings.boundary: Correlation does not show that increasing frustration, friction or distrust causes accuracy. Need-for-cognition subgroups are observational; differential subgroup significance alone does not establish a causal interaction or justify more burdens for a particular group.

methodological_limits: A single low-stakes nutrition substitution task using crowdworkers, not professional clinical decisions or patient outcomes.
No learned AI was trained; recommendation accuracy and error type were controlled by image-recognition omissions and a lookup table.
Flavor similarity is a molecule-overlap score and the optimization target uses a harmonic mean; correct in this task does not establish real taste preference or clinical nutritional appropriateness.
The task requires two discrete choices. Overall-decision accuracy, source detection and wrong-advice agreement are different metrics with different significance patterns.

199 retained participants encountered only two of nine interfaces, with three interfaces unreported. No individual forcing design can be declared superior from the reported nonsignificant within-category comparisons.
Four-item NFC measurement and a median split simplify a continuous construct and were obtained after the first experimental block. A causal moderator or lifelong category cannot be inferred.
The paper reports separately significant effects in high-NFC and nonsignificant effects in low-NFC groups, but these alone are not a formal between-group interaction test.
Pooled decision-frequency chi-square tests include repeated trials; participant-adjusted mixed-model results should be distinguished from treating every trial as an independent person.
Benefits on wrong-advice trials do not amount to significant overall gains against simple explanations; no complete elimination of overreliance was found.
Long-term adoption and intervention-generated inequalities are concerns informed by short-session ratings and subgroup patterns, not observed longitudinal exclusion or uptake.

cross_paper_learning.finding: The Steyvers–Kumar review cites this study. This primary-source reading now supplies exact outcome distinctions; the review citation must not be counted as an independent replication.

Both studies find benefits concentrated on incorrect-advice subsets without significant overall superiority over other collaborative conditions. Their timings, simulations, tasks and correctness definitions differ.
Kupfer invoked cognitive motivation but did not measure NFC. This source supplies a measured individual-difference construct, without retrospectively claiming that it explained Kupfer’s results.

deferred.reason: A family of interventions, not a new psychological behaviour. Store its tested effects within relevant reliance and effort entries.

An outcome-level fairness risk defined by unequal benefit, not a standalone observed intrinsic behaviour of the AI. The short-session median-split analysis is insufficient to establish long-term unequal access.
Already covered by Psychological reactance and only invoked as a rationale here; the primary reactance paper was not independently read.

limitations: One new human motivational construct is indexed with explicit trait/AI boundaries.
The paper’s positive headline is preserved alongside aggregate null comparisons, metric-specific reliance results and secondary-source limits.
